h: The country that went looking for voters now asks voters for proof
dek: Political scientist Milan Vaishnav says SIR has turned free India's basic electoral bargain upside down: getting voters onto the roll used to be the state's job, and now the burden of staying on it falls on the citizen.
body: Milan Vaishnav has written for years about the Election Commission, election funding and defections, and is now preparing a book on how Indian electoral democracy grew. In this piece, published in the Financial Times and repeated on his Substack, his point fits in one sentence: a democracy that once set out in search of the voter is now asking the voter to prove that he belongs here.

The writer reminds us that after 1947 India gave every adult the vote, with no condition of property, literacy or caste. Rolls began to be drawn up even before the Constitution came into force, and the Commission ran door-to-door surveys as far as glaciers, deserts and forests. In many older democracies, getting your name registered is the citizen's responsibility; India gave that duty to the state. Whenever keeping the roll clean clashed with keeping no eligible person out, India always chose to widen the circle.

SIR has reversed this order. More than thirteen crore names have been removed from the draft rolls. The writer accepts that these include deaths, migration and duplicate names, and that some names were also restored, but nobody knows how many eligible people were wrongly left out. The difficulty is that India has no universal document of citizenship; nearly everyone has Aadhaar, but it is treated as proof of identity, not of citizenship. The burden falls heaviest on the poor, women, migrants and minorities.

The numbers from Bengal's April 2026 election are the backbone of the piece. More than 90 lakh names were cut there: 64 lakh as dead, absent, shifted or duplicate, and the remaining 27 lakh on the basis of 'discrepancies' caught by software. More than 80 per cent of people in this second group appealed, but only 1,607 names were restored before the vote. In the appeals that were decided, 93 per cent got their names back, which itself raises a question about the original cuts.

According to Vaishnav, the Commission's strength rests on its reputation for fairness, and charges of bias and reports of disagreement inside the Commission have weakened that reputation. More than 64 crore people voted in the last general election, but the ability to manage that alone does not guarantee an honest election. His final argument stings the most: even if wrongly cut names come back later, the vote that was missed does not come back.
nazar: This piece is not sloganeering but a researcher's cool accounting, and that is why it weighs more. Names returning in 93 per cent of appeals shows that the error was not an exception but the method. A process where the poor citizen carries the burden of being proved wrong, and gets the chance to be proved right only after the election has gone, is not a clean-up. It is a cull.

In our view the debate is now stuck between the slogan of 'vote theft' and the counter-slogan of 'infiltrators', while the real question is constitutional: is the right to vote the state's responsibility or the citizen's test? If the movement from Jantar Mantar to Ramlila Maidan keeps this question alive, it can save something bigger than one officer's resignation.
sawal: Is the right to vote the state's duty or the citizen's test?
ref: Ornit Shani
A historian whose book 'How India Became Democratic' tells how the first voter rolls were made after independence.
Logical discrepancy
'Errors' caught by software during SIR, such as the spelling of a parent's name or a gap in age, on which notices were sent.
ank: names restored in Bengal before the vote

h: Gyanesh Kumar is now a bone stuck in Modi's throat
dek: Senior journalist Maneesh Chhibber says the Chief Election Commissioner has become a burden on the government, yet removing him is no easy deal for it either.
body: For the first time, the opposition has run an 'impeachment' of a Chief Election Commissioner in the people's court, and on 1 November Ramlila Maidan drew a crowd that some are calling the biggest since 1974. Chhibber says public pressure over Gyanesh Kumar and SIR is growing, not easing.

The writer sees Modi as a leader who reads the wind quickly. In his view the Prime Minister must have understood that Gyanesh Kumar is weighing down not only his government but his own image. Things have reached a point where even loyal BJP supporters no longer defend him; the writer suggests taking a look at your own family WhatsApp group. Even anchors of the godi media (TV channels seen as lapdogs of the government) have started asking the Commission questions, while Delhi Police is cracking down on peaceful Gen Z protesters.

In Chhibber's view, even the ordinary person who has little to do with politics now believes the Commissioner works at the ruling party's signal. No explanation, no new story is working. So his conclusion is clear: Gyanesh Kumar's time is up.

But this is where the real knot lies. Removing a minister is easy, as when Dharmendra Pradhan had to go under pressure from the Cockroach Janata Party and the opposition. The Chief Election Commissioner heads an institution considered independent. His resignation under pressure would raise questions about every election held under his watch. On top of that, the writer feels the movement will not stop here, and its next target will be higher.
The government has one more worry: what message would go to the officers and policemen who bend rules to please their masters. The writer says this is the real test of Modi's political sense.
nazar: Chhibber's analysis shows both the strength of the movement and its limit. If the government does not remove Gyanesh Kumar only because it would raise questions about past results, it means it is protecting its results more than the institution's credibility. And if it does remove him, the questions will not end; they will only change address. The account of thirteen crore cut names is not settled by one chair falling empty.
sawal: If an officer is costly to protect, how costly is it to remove him?
ref: Removing the Chief Election Commissioner
Under Article 324 of the Constitution, the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only in the same way as a Supreme Court judge, that is, by a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.
People's impeachment
A symbolic event by the INDIA alliance in which the charges against Gyanesh Kumar were read out and a 'verdict' given. It has no legal standing; it is a form of political protest.

h: Protest is not only anger, it is also the joy of telling the truth
dek: The writer sees the Ramlila Maidan rally as a people's play whose energy came from ordinary people, not leaders, and calls the government's counter-rallies a confession of weakness.
body: Varsha Tiwari's piece begins with a simple idea: a public protest is a collective refusal to accept a lie, and that refusal carries a special kind of joy. She saw this joy in the crowd moving towards Ramlila Maidan on 1 November. Groups from Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Rajasthan and the Northeast, youth and women's organisations, arrived from the direction of Minto Bridge, the railway station and Mir Dard Chowk with banners, flags and drums.

She writes that people watched the procession from buses, trees, walls and the rooftops of government colonies. She asks whether the ruling leaders sitting in nearby offices heard the noise. In her view the presence of the INDIA alliance gave a ring of safety, but the energy belonged to ordinary citizens, whose demands were free and fair elections, electoral justice and transparency.

The second part of the piece is about the ruling side's response. She says the BJP took out counter-marches under the name 'Save democracy, remove anarchy', one of them in Chandni Chowk. She says calling protest 'anarchy' is an old method of governments, and so is the argument about traders losing money at Diwali. She calls the half-hearted workers and song programmes of the counter-marches 'a quiet confession of their own weakness'.

She remembers Shaheen Bagh, the farmers at the Tikri border and the wrestlers dragged on Parliament Street: such resistance is remembered even in defeat. For her, AISA president Neha Bora questioning from the stage the demand to prove citizenship, the SFI's slogans to the beat of the daphli (a hand drum), and the long printed list of cut names are the marks of this 'festival of truth'.

Her conclusion is that repression such as detention, harassment and the loss of jobs only makes protesters dig in harder, and that the young have understood that the price of freedom is paid in sweat, blood, spray paint and memes.
nazar: This is not a report but a scene written through a sympathiser's eyes, and it should be read that way. Still, the piece catches one important thing: the counter-marches show that this crowd on the street is making power uneasy. When a government starts borrowing the opposition's methods, the debate moves away from the issue and becomes a contest of spectacle.

Joy is the fuel of a movement, not its destination. In our view the next test is how the energy of Ramlila Maidan reaches concrete demands such as restoring cut names and holding the Commission accountable.
sawal: Are counter-marches a sign of strength or of nervousness?
ref: AISA
All India Students' Association, a left student organisation whose president Neha Bora is a well-known voice of this movement.
Mir Dard Chowk
A crossing near Old Delhi named after Khwaja Mir Dard, the eighteenth-century Sufi poet.

h: A letter from 124 former officers, and the Commission's quiet retreat
dek: Retired IAS officer Avay Shukla says the Election Commission's own recent steps are disproving the letter written in Gyanesh Kumar's defence.
body: 124 former bureaucrats have written an open letter defending Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and SIR. Avay Shukla, himself a former IAS officer, calls this letter standing on the wrong side of history. This column is an edited version of a post from his blog, published in Urdu in Qaumi Awaz.

Shukla says bureaucrats are usually timid people who stand with power, and he suspects that posts, favours or fear of a chargesheet lie behind these signatures. He alleges that many of the signatories are either unknown or have been linked to the BJP and right-wing bodies. For him the letter is nothing more than flattery of the Commission, and is really a reply to the earlier letters of the Constitutional Conduct Group.

The most interesting part of the argument is the list the writer draws up from the Commission's decisions of the past two weeks. According to him, the doubtful declaration attached to Form 6 was quietly dropped, electoral registration officers got access to ECI-Net back, a technical committee was set up to examine the software, a limit was fixed on how many Form 7s one person can file in bulk, and a drive was run to add back wrongly cut names.

The writer also says a special summary revision has begun in seventeen states for eighteen-year-olds who were left out, candidates will get machine-readable rolls, and parties will get the full list of names cut and added. Most important, in his view the Commission has indirectly admitted that it has no data to prove that the thirteen crore cut names were 'infiltrators'.

Shukla compares this to an accused confessing in court: these are the very demands on which the opposition and civil society had been standing firm for months. In his eyes the letter is not dissent but support for taking away the vote on a large scale.
nazar: The real strength of this column lies not in its abuse but in that list. If the Commission itself is taking, one by one, the very steps that people were demanding while being beaten with lathis at Jantar Mantar, it is fair to ask who paid the price of the stubbornness so far. The same question goes to the retired officers signing in support of power: when will their pens move for the lakhs of people whose names were cut without proof?
sawal: If the Form 6 declaration has been dropped, why was it added in the first place?
ref: Constitutional Conduct Group
A group of former bureaucrats who for about ten years have been writing open letters to the government on constitutional values and the independence of institutions.
Form 6 and Form 7
Form 6 is filled to add a new name to the voter roll; Form 7 is used to object to a name and get it removed.

h: The INDIA alliance after Ramlila: a big chance, a long road
dek: The writer says the rally of more than nineteen parties was not just a gathering, but adds that to turn anger into change the alliance must go beyond Delhi to towns, villages and campuses.
body: Ranjan Solomon sees the 1 November rally at Ramlila Maidan as a turning point. More than nineteen opposition parties were on one stage, and leaders such as Rahul Gandhi, Mallikarjun Kharge, Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav and Farooq Abdullah recognised a big challenge despite their rivalries. The writer says the BJP's 'invincible' image is manufactured, and beneath it anger is building over unemployment, inequality, the decay of institutions and the crushing of dissent.

The writer says the promise of development is in question: the young are struggling with insecure jobs, students with exam irregularities, farmers with costs and workers with rising prices. In his view religious mobilisation cannot take the place of jobs, education, health and social security.

The writer sees SIR as the opposition's most solid democratic issue. Mentioning reports of more than thirteen crore names being cut, he also gives the Commission's side, that these were dead, duplicate, absent or permanently moved voters. His demand is transparency, an independent inquiry and easy appeals, and he tells the opposition to record the irregularities, take the legal route and make sure no eligible citizen loses the vote.

The writer credits Rahul Gandhi with giving a clear story on constitutional protection, electoral transparency and institutional accountability, but also says the alliance is bigger than any one leader, and regional partners such as Mamata Banerjee and Akhilesh Yadav are just as important. Instead of relying only on an anti-incumbency wave, it needs an alternative model of governance tied to economic justice.

In the end he writes that the rally showed the country has not handed over its democratic future, but if this energy stays in Delhi, it will scatter. Taking it to towns, villages, universities and workplaces and building solid electoral alliances is the real work.
nazar: The piece is full of hope, at places more than needed, and the prediction of the BJP's 'fall' is the writer's own opinion, not evidence. But its most useful point is simple: a rally lasts a day, organisation is daily. The INDIA alliance has set up big stages before and then broken apart over seat sharing.

In our view the test this time will be whether the parties on the stage are seen working booth by booth to restore names cut in SIR. The fight to save the vote is won not by speeches but by getting forms filled.
sawal: Will the unity on the stage reach the booth, or fall apart again?
ref: INDIA alliance
A front of opposition parties formed in 2023 against the BJP, including the Congress, Trinamool, SP, the Left parties and others.
Countercurrents
An English website run from Kerala that publishes pieces on social movements from a left-liberal view.

h: The map of 2029 in the Ramlila rally
dek: Open's political editor sees the 'vote theft' slogan as no longer one rally but a strategy that will run until the next Lok Sabha election, though it still has to reach the voter.
body: On Sunday, in a rain-soaked Ramlila Maidan, Rahul Gandhi repeated what he has been saying for months: elections have been stolen for years, and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar stands with the BJP. He named Madhya Pradesh, Haryana, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Karnataka and the 2024 Lok Sabha election as links in this chain.

Rahul's calculation was that after 2024 about thirteen and a half crore names, or nearly fifteen per cent of voters, were removed from the rolls, while the gap between the NDA and the Congress was only three per cent. On this basis he called the last general election illegal and declared that the Commissioner would go to jail and that the Prime Minister and Home Minister would also have to leave their seats.

The writer says these claims can be checked, but the real point is strategy. The INDIA alliance is building a story of 'democratic backsliding' by questioning the legitimacy of BJP wins, and is giving this campaign legal legs by challenging SIR again and again in court. The BJP replied by alleging anarchy and an attempt to overturn the government.

The writer also reminds us that SIR did not become a big issue in the state elections, except in Bengal. In Tamil Nadu the DMK stayed silent during the campaign and blamed SIR after losing, while the winning TVK also said that it would have won more seats if the rolls had not been tampered with.

His view of the crowd is that it was quite large but smaller than claimed. Left party flags were the most numerous, then the Samajwadi Party's, and fewer of the Congress, though the draw was Rahul himself. By his reckoning the people who came were angrier about the exclusion they feel economically and socially than about the details of 'vote theft'. The Congress's challenge is to turn this anger into votes, and the fight will stay hot until Parliament's winter session.
nazar: This piece looks at the rally from a spot close to the ruling side, and still admits one important thing: the people in the ground came not for any one figure but with a feeling of being shut out. A name cut from the voter roll is the most concrete form of that feeling.

In our view a bigger question than counting the crowd and sorting the flags is when, and before whom, the Commission will account for the more than thirteen crore cut names. Until that answer comes, whether 'vote theft' is a slogan or a strategy, the doubt is sure to take root on the ground.
sawal: Is asking for an account of cut names a strategy or a right?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision, in which the voter roll is made afresh and every voter has to prove eligibility again.
Winter session
Parliament's last session of the year, which usually runs from late November into December.
ank: names cut after 2024, according to Rahul Gandhi
gap between NDA and Congress votes in 2024

h: If the old Form 6 is back, why was SIR needed?
dek: The Commission itself has admitted that names can be added through the normal process after SIR; the writer asks why, then, crores of people were put through a heavy test of documents.
body: This piece by activist and independent journalist Shivasundar takes apart the Commission's 'unanimous' decision that came on 26 September, after the Indian Express reported the dissent of two Election Commissioners. The writer asks why decisions that took two hours could not find time in ten months. In his view these decisions are an unspoken admission of past mistakes.

The decisions said that voters with a 'logical discrepancy' would not be called to offices; officials would go to their homes. Meeting agendas would be circulated in advance and minutes afterwards. The writer calls these welcome but basic, and says they suggest the Chief Election Commissioner had not been following these rules so far. Under the 1995 law, the three-member Commission has to decide by consensus or majority, so decisions taken without a shared agenda raise questions of legality.

The writer says that in Bengal 1.4 crore notices went out from the centre without informing the local electoral registration officers. 38 lakh cases reached the tribunals, of which 16 lakh were filed by the Commission itself against people whose claims had already been accepted. The writer alleges that about 90 per cent of these were against Muslims. In Goa, 97 names were not added despite an officer's order.

The sharpest argument is about Form 6. The Commission added its new conditions in July 2026, that is, after the Supreme Court's 27 May judgment, so the writer finds the claim of the court's approval only half true. Now the Commission itself says that people left out after SIR is complete can get their names added through the normal 'continuous updation', with a paper such as Aadhaar.

The writer asks: if the back door was open, who was the heavy front door for, and what will happen to the fourteen crore people who are already out? The piece ends with ten demands, including scrapping SIR and the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner.
nazar: This piece is five weeks old but more relevant today, when the Commission is talking about a normal revision in place of SIR in the remaining seventeen states. The writer's question is direct, and the Commission has not answered it yet: if the ordinary route was enough, why was an extraordinary sieve put in place?

Many of the piece's figures and charges rest on the writer's own estimates and newspaper reports, and some of the ten demands, such as cancelling all elections, are political demands, not findings of an inquiry. But the argument about the Form 6 dates stands on paper, and the Supreme Court should look at it in the next hearing.
sawal: If the back door was open, who was the heavy door built for?
ref: Form 6
The application to become a new voter or get a name added again, to which an extra declaration and documents were added during SIR.
Electoral Registration Officer (ERO)
The local officer who, under the law, has the final power to add or remove a name from the roll.

h: US midterms: the bigger test is accepting the result, not the count
dek: Washington journalist Said Arikat says the 3 November vote will decide how far courts, officials and Congress can rein in Trump's power.
body: America holds its midterm elections today, and the writer does not see them as only a fight for seats in Congress. In his view the real question is whether the Constitution's checks on President Donald Trump's power still work, whether the officials who run elections can withstand pressure, and whether the government will accept a result that goes against it.

Courts have so far put up a good deal of resistance on election rules. According to a Brennan Center review of 20 October, at least 34 federal court rulings have blocked the administration's election moves or its demands for voter records, and these rulings came from judges appointed by presidents of both parties, including judges appointed by Trump himself. But courts often wake up only after a step has already been taken. The Justice Department's demand to set aside the ballots of about 20 thousand California voters is still hanging.
The writer draws a line: investigating real wrongdoing is one thing, and stopping lawful voters on mere suspicion is another. Repeated noise about fraud, even without evidence, hollows out trust.

If the Democrats win the House, scrutiny of immigration, spending and executive orders will sharpen, and if they win the Senate, appointments will be affected, but Trump will keep the veto and executive power. The most delicate stretch comes after the voting. It is important to remember the fraud claims after the 2020 defeat, the pressure on Georgia's officials and the attack on the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The writer's conclusion is that courts alone cannot save democracy, because they do not run elections in thousands of counties. The test is simply that votes are counted by law and the result is respected, because no president is above the law.
nazar: Even the world's most powerful democracy stands today before the question of whether the loser will accept defeat. In India too there is a debate over voter rolls and the voter's rights, so the American courts' stand is worth remembering: no lawful citizen's vote can be taken away in the name of suspicion.
sawal: Can courts watch over thousands of polling stations?
ref: Midterm elections
Elections held in America midway through the president's four-year term, in which all seats of the House of Representatives and a third of the Senate are at stake.
Brennan Center
A legal research institute linked to New York University that keeps watch on voting rights and election laws.

h: Might is right: an account of a crumbling world order
dek: Using Gideon Rachman's new book, Maleeha Lodhi explains why the world is in its most restless phase since the Cold War, and why South Asia cannot be ignored.
body: Maleeha Lodhi, Pakistan's former ambassador (to the US, the UK and the United Nations), writes that the world today is in its most unstable state since the Cold War. The old framework, with whatever rules it had, has broken. Force has again become the first weapon, and diplomacy is often remembered only after the missiles have been fired.

The figures are frightening. The war between the US and Israel on one side and Iran on the other, the fighting between Ukraine and Russia, Israel's war on Gaza and its attacks on its neighbours. A Swedish university counted 65 active conflicts in 2025, the largest number of conflicts between states since the Second World War.

Against this background Lodhi reads the book by the Financial Times's Gideon Rachman. Rachman lists three reasons: a shifting balance of power that challenges American dominance, the rise of strongmen who see war as legitimate, and the resulting decay of international law. Putin, Trump and Netanyahu are on his list, and Trump's revival of the Monroe Doctrine is an example of 'spheres of influence' thinking.

Lodhi does not agree with everything. Calling Russia, China, North Korea and Iran an 'axis of upheaval' seems exaggerated to her, because these countries' interests are not the same and the book does not prove solid ties between them. For a third world war Rachman sets the condition of a direct clash between great powers and fighting that spreads across continents, which has not yet happened, but is not impossible either.

Lodhi finds the book's chapter on the four-day India-Pakistan clash of May 2025 especially striking. Rachman warns that each time, more advanced weapons have been used between the two nuclear neighbours, and that the world pays too little attention to South Asia.
nazar: When great powers make breaking the rules normal, small countries and ordinary people pay the heaviest price. The lesson for India and Pakistan is clear: war fever between neighbours with nuclear weapons is no game, and talking of peace is not weakness but good sense.
sawal: Amid sixty-five wars, who will talk of peace?
ref: Monroe Doctrine
The policy declared in 1823 by US President James Monroe, under which the whole American continent was treated as Washington's zone of influence.

h: Bangladesh: save the rivers in the manifesto, factories on the riverbank in the gazette
dek: Kallol Mustafa says the BNP government makes a lot of noise about planting trees, but its decisions on the Buriganga, the ship-breaking industry and the Sundarbans go the other way.
body: Kallol Mustafa, an engineer who writes on energy and the environment, says the environmental promises and decisions of Bangladesh's BNP government are clashing with each other. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman talks about rivers and forests, and tree planting and river dredging programmes are visible too, but something else is being written on paper.

The manifesto promised to curb Dhaka's pollution, to turn low-lying areas into water retention zones and a 'green canal bank model' for riverbanks. In September the Prime Minister also ordered that pollution of the rivers around the capital be stopped. But on 14 October a gazette from the housing ministry changed the Detailed Area Plan: heavy industry was allowed on open land along the Buriganga, and protection for areas where floodwater flows was ended. No technical process was followed and no one was consulted.

There was a promise to make the ship-breaking industry green, but on 29 September a committee chaired by Environment Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo moved it from the 'red' to the 'orange' category at the yard owners' demand. This could remove the requirement of an environmental impact assessment for new yards. The committee had no environmental expert.

The biggest danger is to the Sundarbans. According to reports, the government wants to build a floating LNG terminal at Akram Point and a pipeline to Mongla. This spot is within two kilometres of two wildlife sanctuaries included in a UNESCO World Heritage site. The noise of ships, dirty water and dredging threaten the Irrawaddy and Ganges dolphins and the breathing roots of the mangroves. The fire at the Maheshkhali LNG terminal in July and past oil spills make this fear real.

The writer also asks why a third, costly terminal is needed when not enough gas is arriving even for the two existing ones. His conclusion is that the promises will come true only if the ministries reverse these decisions.
nazar: The Sundarbans are a shared heritage of India and Bangladesh; their dolphins and fishermen do not recognise a border. This game of giving pollution a free pass under the slogan of 'green development' is familiar in India too, where environmental clearance is often seen as an obstacle to business.
sawal: How far from the LNG terminal must a dolphin go to be safe?
ref: Sundarbans
The world's largest mangrove forest, in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, divided between India and Bangladesh, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
LNG terminal
A place where liquefied natural gas brought by ships is stored, turned back into gas and sent into pipelines.

h: Egypt: sit on the licence file, then fine them for having no licence
dek: In Global Voices, Walid El Houri describes how a sentence and an order to shut the outlet came down on Mada Masr editor Lina Attalah in a single hearing.
body: The grip on free media in Egypt keeps tightening. The writer says it began with 'Matsda2sh', a team of six young journalists who checked online claims using social media and open sources. Team members were made to disappear for several days and questioned in illegal detention, there are allegations of torture, and they are now in pre-trial detention on charges of terrorism and false news.

Then came the turn of Mada Masr and its founder-editor Lina Attalah. On 27 October, in a single hearing, a court convicted her of running a news website without a licence and imposed the maximum fine of three million Egyptian pounds, about 55 thousand dollars. She was taken from the court by force and held for seven hours until the fine was paid. The court also ordered the website shut and its equipment seized. Mada Masr says eight of her lawyers were present, yet the judge appointed a lawyer of his own.

The irony is that, according to Amnesty International, Mada Masr applied for a licence in 2018 and 2020 and got no reply, and applied again in 2026. Now there is a second case on 11 November on the charge of false news, which could bring prison.

Founded in 2013, Mada Masr has written about torture survivors, political prisoners, reproductive rights, the wars in Sudan and Gaza, refugees and internet freedom. According to the CPJ, at least 25 journalists are in prison in Egypt. The outlet has said it will keep publishing every day while it looks for a legal way forward, and a joint statement led by Amnesty has condemned the ruling.
The writer's conclusion is that a licensing system in which applications lie untouched for years is a tool of censorship, and press freedom in Egypt is not possible without ending it.
nazar: First refuse permission, then punish people for working without permission: this method does not belong to Cairo alone. In India too, pressure on independent digital media through rules, raids and lawsuits has grown. Standing with Mada Masr means standing with free journalism across the Global South.
sawal: If an application goes unanswered for eight years, who is the guilty one?
ref: Mada Masr
An independent Egyptian news outlet started in 2013 by Lina Attalah, published in Arabic and English, and blocked in the country since 2017.
CPJ
The Committee to Protect Journalists, a New York body that keeps count of arrests and killings of journalists around the world.
photo_note: Representative image: a newspaper printing press

h: Journalism in Pakistan: a record written in the shadow of death
dek: Arifa Noor reads the new book by journalist and union leader Mazhar Abbas, which records the press's struggle in Pakistan, its divisions and the killing of journalists.
body: Arifa Noor is a full-time journalist herself, and says the difficulties of the profession never leave her mind. That is why Mazhar Abbas's book 'Media Under the Shadow of Death' feels special to her. Abbas has been both a journalist and part of journalist union politics, and in her view he is one of the few who did both jobs honestly.

The book tells the story of the unions from Pakistan's early years: the Sindh Union of Journalists, the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists (PFUJ), and journalists' resistance to undemocratic regimes. Arifa spots two patterns that keep returning. First, rivalry among journalists and political partisanship, which governments kept using, such as the journalists who asked General Zia to put off elections. Second, owners giving in quickly under pressure, such as signing a code of conduct during Musharraf's emergency.

The strongest part is about the Musharraf years, when the media grew and violence against journalists grew too. Political parties, lawyers and journalists then stood together against the military ruler. Abbas calls this the PFUJ's last united fight, but does not explain why the union fell apart, which the writer misses.

The second important part is about the killing of journalists. The case of Wali Babar is chilling: when the trial moved forward, the investigating officer, the public prosecutor and witnesses were killed too. Along with well-known cases such as Hayatullah Khan, Musa Khankhel and Arshad Sharif, there are less known names as well.
Arifa sees the book as more a reference work than an analysis, one whose language and editing needed more work, but whose information is valuable.
nazar: On this side of the border too, the killing of journalists, owners' compromises and weakening unions are no unknown story. This book reminds us that press freedom survives only when journalists drop their rivalries and stand together.
sawal: When even the witnesses are killed, what can justice lean on?
ref: PFUJ
Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists, the national journalists' union formed in 1950, which led many movements against military regimes.
Wali Babar
A Geo News reporter killed in Karachi in 2011; several witnesses and investigators were also killed during the trial.
photo_note: Terrible news, a satirical drawing by Gaganendranath Tagore

h: Data law: the fraudster's permission before probing the fraud?
dek: Meghna Bal and Shweta Venkatesan say the Digital Personal Data Protection law makes journalism harder, weighs heavily on small business and gives government surveillance a free hand.
body: Twenty-one publishers have challenged the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) in court. Their argument is that this law gives journalism no exemption, which means a person's consent is needed before using their personal information in a story. The writers' example is simple: if you need to look at the accused's transactions while probing a financial fraud, first take permission from that same person. That makes investigative journalism almost impossible.

But the damage is not limited to the media. This law applies to every sector, and following it is costly: mapping data, systems for notice and consent, systems for correction and deletion. Consulting firms estimate the first-year cost at 10 lakh to 1.5 crore rupees for startups and small businesses, 35 lakh to 2.5 crore for mid-sized companies and 1.5 to 18 crore rupees for large companies.

A survey of 330 firms in Shivamogga, Karnataka, found average first-year earnings of about 12.2 lakh rupees, which means even the lowest estimated cost would eat up more than 80 per cent of their income. On top of that, people who make products will get tied up in paperwork compliance. Even an ordinary activity like marketing has no exemption, so how are small sellers to reach customers?
By contrast, the law is soft on what citizens fear most, which is government surveillance. Police and investigating agencies have broad exemptions, and the government can exempt any agency.

The writers also question the process: the 2022 draft came out for public comment, but the changed version brought to Parliament in 2023 was passed without any scrutiny. In their view the publishers' petition is a chance to fix the law's basic flaws.
nazar: A law made in the name of the ordinary citizen's privacy ties down the journalist and the small shopkeeper and leaves the government free. It looks less like protecting privacy and more like guarding information, and it will hit first the stories that ask the powerful for an account.
sawal: Why should a Shivamogga shopkeeper hand over eighty per cent of his earnings?
ref: DPDPA
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: India's personal data protection law, whose rules were notified in 2025.

h: The government's 'secular' argument against a hundred-year-old mosque
dek: The Centre told the Delhi High Court that the old mosque at Krishi Bhawan does not fit the secular character of a government complex, and so will be removed.
body: The central government has told the Delhi High Court in an affidavit that the Qadeemi Masjid (old mosque), about a hundred years old and standing in the open courtyard of Krishi Bhawan, will be demolished. The government argues that Krishi Bhawan and the Central Secretariat are meant only for administrative and public service work, and keeping a religious structure there does not fit the secular character of the complex.

Krishi Bhawan and the nearby Shastri Bhawan are to be pulled down under the Central Vista project. The Centre says it is not possible to leave room for any religious structure in the new master plan, and for prayers there is the Shahi Masjid Zabta Ganj near India Gate, about two kilometres away. On Monday Justice Anish Dayal had asked the government whether any rule bars a place of worship in government complexes.

The committee that looks after the mosque went to court in September. It says employees of Krishi Bhawan and nearby offices have been offering namaz here for decades, and the Delhi Waqf Board declared it waqf property in 1970. The committee has asked that if saving the mosque is truly impossible, at least another site be given.

In 2021, when the Waqf Board sought protection for six mosques in the project's path, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta had assured the court that nothing would happen to these properties. The mosque was missing from the maps in a tender issued in January this year. The next hearing in the case is on 23 November.
nazar: The secularism cited to remove a mosque is never applied to the pujas held daily in government offices or to the bhoomi pujan (ground-breaking rites) of new buildings. If an assurance given in court in 2021 can change in five years, it is a warning for the other waqf properties too.
sawal: Where has the 2021 assurance to the court gone now?
ref: Central Vista
The Centre's project to remake Delhi's Rajpath area, begun in 2019, under which a new Parliament building and new government offices are being built.
Waqf property
Land or a building dedicated forever to religious or charitable work, looked after by a Waqf Board.

h: A dam on the Kulsi: the dolphin's home and the Khasi villages' 'no'
dek: More than two dozen villages on both sides of the Assam-Meghalaya border are holding sit-ins against a proposed 55 megawatt dam, while the state government pushes ahead.
body: Amid the debate over the big dam in Arunachal, protest against another dam on the Assam-Meghalaya border has grown sharper. A 55 megawatt multipurpose project is proposed on the Kulsi river, with an estimated cost of about 1,454.95 crore rupees. According to the Jal Shakti ministry, it will irrigate 26,000 hectares, generate power and reduce the risk of floods.

The dam is to be built at Ukiam, where three hill streams meet. The 62 metre high dam will drown most of the homes in Ukiam, where about 800 people live. The official estimate puts the affected villages at about 15, while the communities' own survey counts 36 villages on both sides of the border. In July the project report was handed to Assam's power company.

More than 26 villages have held sit-ins, submitted memorandums and protested in Guwahati. Sengjan Sangma, president of the Kulsi River Valley Protection Committee, alleges that Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma broke his promise not to build the dam without public consent. In October the headmen of three Khasi villages refused to give consent, and Hima Rambrai had passed a resolution back in 2013 not to dam the rivers of its area.

The Kulsi is home to the Ganges dolphin, called shihu here. The 2022 national survey recorded about 20 dolphins in the Kukurmara stretch. The dam site is just three kilometres from Chandubi lake, and people have listed at least 12 wetlands that could be affected. No independent environmental assessment has been made public so far.
nazar: In the Northeast the map of development is often drawn in Delhi or Guwahati, and the Adivasi (indigenous) villages along the river are told later. Where the consent of traditional institutions is part of both the Constitution and custom, brushing aside their 'no' is a question not only of the environment but of trust.
sawal: Who asked the shihu dolphin whether the river should be dammed?
ref: Hima
The traditional unit of government in Khasi society, a group of several villages, whose head is called the Syiem.
Ganges dolphin
A nearly blind freshwater dolphin, India's national aquatic animal, which survives only in clean, flowing rivers.

h: The hands that sew the world's clothes, hungry at home
dek: Bangladesh's garment workers stayed on the streets for a third day demanding a rise in the minimum wage from 12,500 to 30,000 taka, and police fired tear gas.
body: Laily Begum, 37, who runs a sewing machine in a factory near Dhaka, earns about 15,000 taka a month, 18 to 20 thousand with overtime. On this, her two children have had to drop out of school, and many times no proper meal is cooked at home. This Al Jazeera report shows, in the words of such workers, the movement that has been going on since 1 November.

About 40 lakh people work in Bangladesh's garment industry, half of them women. More than 80 per cent of the country's export earnings come from it, 39 billion dollars last year. The minimum wage now is 12,500 taka, and workers are asking for 30,000. In Cambodia it is about 210 dollars a month; in Bangladesh, about 102 dollars.

On the third day police in Ashulia fired tear gas and stun grenades, and dozens were arrested. According to the owners' association, work stopped at 529 factories on Sunday, affecting about ten lakh workers. Roads were blocked in Gazipur and vehicles were set on fire.

The government has formed a six-member wage board, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held an emergency meeting. Inflation was 8.34 per cent in September, and the last wage rise came in December 2023. Owners say wages can rise if international brands pay fair prices, while researchers point out that the bigger share of the profit stays with Western buyers.
nazar: From Tiruppur to Noida, the story of India's garment workers is not very different. As long as global brands keep playing one country against another for cheap stitching, the fight over wages will remain a shared fight across borders.
sawal: How much did the person who sewed a shirt worth thousands get?
ref: Ashulia
An industrial area north-west of Dhaka with hundreds of garment factories.
Wage board
A committee of government, owner and worker representatives that sets the minimum wage for an industry.

h: Jantar Mantar is 'just a road', Delhi Police tells the court
dek: In an affidavit to the Supreme Court, the police commissioner said Jantar Mantar should never have been made a protest site, and that Ramlila Maidan, the CBD Ground and Burari are now the options.
body: Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar has filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court defending the decision to remove Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites. The police say no one has an absolute right to protest at a particular place, and that Jantar Mantar is a public road that should never have been made a protest site in the first place. The reply came in the case of Swati Singh vs Union of India.

According to the police, the decision followed the recommendation of a Home Ministry committee formed on 26 August 2026, which unanimously found the place unsuitable. Three sites have been offered instead: Ramlila Maidan in central Delhi, the CBD Ground in east Delhi and the Burari Ground in the north-west. The affidavit also says that in the age of technology and social media, the need to protest near the seat of power has ended.

Figures are listed too: more than 1,300 protests a year take place at Jantar Mantar, its capacity is about 1,500 people, and on 20 July 2026 the crowd went beyond this. The police cited the 78 embassies, 99 government offices, the new Parliament building and Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital nearby.
In a separate affidavit, the police said Mamata Banerjee and Derek O'Brien were removed from South Avenue for breaking prohibitory orders, not detained.
nazar: The very meaning of protest is to make power hear you face to face. Protest sent off to the Burari ground does not reach the government's window, and the argument that 'social media is enough' comes from the same police who are sending notices to shut down online accounts. In the middle of a movement against the Election Commission, this decision does not look like a coincidence.
sawal: If a protest cannot be heard in Parliament, how much of it is left?
ref: Jantar Mantar
An eighteenth-century observatory in Delhi built by Sawai Jai Singh; the road beside it has been the country's main protest site since 1993.
Section 163, Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita
The section of the new criminal procedure code that lets the administration ban gatherings in an area, replacing the old Section 144.

h: Digital rights groups' accounts targeted in the name of 'defamation'
dek: Delhi Police has sent two notices to X asking it to take down the accounts of the Internet Freedom Foundation, SFLC and GeoBlockedIndia.
body: Delhi Police has sent two notices to X demanding the removal of two digital rights organisations, the Internet Freedom Foundation and the Software Freedom Law Centre, and of an account called GeoBlockedIndia. The charge is defamation of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The notices were sent by the Special Commissioner (Crime) on 31 October and 2 November.

The two notices together have 40 links: three accounts and 37 posts, including 16 posts by other people. The police have cited Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which deals with criminal defamation. The matter began on 29 October, when these organisations received an alleged legal notice on behalf of the RSS asking them to stop opposing blocking orders. Several Sangh office-bearers had questioned whether that notice was even genuine.

The IFF says criminal defamation is not an offence where the police can step in directly, and there is neither a complaint from the RSS nor a magistrate's order. Shutting down an entire account over a few posts is a far harsher step than needed, since the posts only criticised that very notice.

The organisation says that in the three weeks before the first notice it helped 86 people whose accounts or posts were blocked. SFLC's tracker recorded blocks on about 268 pieces of content and 83 accounts in the first 29 days of October. X sent the notices to the IFF on 3 November but did not say whether it had acted on them. The IFF has said it will go to court if the notices are not withdrawn.
nazar: The organisations that work to get other people's blocked accounts restored are now themselves being silenced. This is not the case of two organisations alone: if the police can get an entire account removed without a complaint and without a court order, any critic could be next.
sawal: Why should an account be shut on a complaint no complainant made?
ref: Internet Freedom Foundation
A Delhi non-governmental organisation that fights legal battles on online speech, privacy and internet shutdowns.
Section 356, Nyaya Sanhita
The section on criminal defamation in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, under which the complaint is usually filed in court by the aggrieved person or body itself.

h: A viral video, and a Mumbai mall's prayer room is gone
dek: After an online campaign and protests by Sakal Hindu Samaj, the prayer room at Inorbit Mall in Malad was torn down.
body: A Muslim prayer room inside Inorbit Mall in Mumbai's Malad area has been torn down after opposition from the Hindutva group Sakal Hindu Samaj. The row began with a viral video in which two girls wearing hijabs showed the room. They urged people not to skip their daily prayers and pointed out that it had separate sections for men and women and a place for wudu (ablution).

Right-wing accounts targeted the video and asked why a shopping mall had a space for namaz. On 30 October, Sakal Hindu Samaj posted the video on X, asked why a mall used by people of every faith had a separate place of worship, called it a mosque and called a protest to have it removed.

On 31 October the group shared another video, which it said showed the room before and after removal. The group claimed a 'secret mosque' had been built in the mall and was brought down after protests by Hindu residents. According to the report, it is not clear who carried out the demolition, and the mall has made no statement.

The report points out that malls and offices often set up prayer rooms for visitors and staff. Earlier, BJP leader Kirit Somaiya ran a campaign against a mosque near Terminal 2 of Mumbai airport, which the MMRDA later declared unauthorised and ordered removed.
nazar: A few people bowing their heads in a small room harmed no one. Yet two days of online noise wiped out a place of prayer on private premises, and neither the mall nor the administration said a word. When mob pressure becomes the rule, any shared space can be the next target.
sawal: Why did the mall quietly give in to the pressure?
ref: Sakal Hindu Samaj
A platform of Hindutva groups active in Maharashtra, which has held rallies on issues such as conversion and 'love jihad'.
Prayer room
A small space in airports, malls and offices where travellers or staff can pray for a short while.

h: Ruby Ali Khan at Jantar Mantar: I will not be afraid
dek: A migrant woman from Bihar, whose seven relatives' names were cut from the voter roll, came to the 2 October protest and went all the way to the police station for detained students.
body: On Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October 2026, a protest was held at Delhi's Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and a review of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter roll. Students, retired officers and leaders of several parties took part. In this crowd was Ruby Ali Khan, in her forties, who came to Delhi from Bihar about thirty years ago.

Ruby's own name is on the roll, but the names of seven of her relatives and many neighbours have been cut. The name of her widowed sister, who has three children, is also missing, and she now fears losing her ration card. Ruby herself depends on free ration from the public distribution system, so for her the question is not only about the vote but about food.

Getting there was not easy. Changing two metros, a bus and two autos, she arrived at half past ten in the morning. She says the main metro stations had been shut to stop people. On Ashoka Road police parked private buses and packed protesters into them, and by evening more than five hundred people had been arrested.

Bindiya (name changed), a 24-year-old student at a south Delhi college, was detained at one in the afternoon and held for six hours. She says about forty students were given neither food nor water. Worried about these girls, Ruby went all the way to the faraway Dwarka police station and stayed there until they were released at seven in the evening.

Ruby says that in today's India being a woman and being a Muslim are both hard. She knows the price of speaking up could be a bulldozer at her home or a beating for her husband and sons. Still, she says she will not be afraid, because she came for those girls, who deserve a better country.
nazar: The debate over names cut from the voter roll often shrinks into figures. Ruby's story shows that one cut name shakes ration, identity and safety, all three at once.
In a democracy where metros are shut to keep people from reaching a peaceful protest and students are kept hungry and thirsty, women like Ruby standing firm is the strongest testimony of all.
sawal: Why do ration and citizenship start to wobble the moment a name is cut?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision, the Election Commission process in which the voter roll is checked afresh. There is controversy over names being removed on a large scale under it.
Public distribution system
The government system of giving cheap or free grain through ration cards, on which crores of poor families depend.

h: A march in Bangkok by people uprooted by dams and mines
dek: Police stopped farmers, fishers and indigenous communities on their way to protest the annual meeting of the World Bank and the IMF.
body: The annual meeting of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund was being held in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand. At the same time, people linked to the 'People's Network against the World Bank and IMF' were marching towards the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center. Police stopped them at the Rama 4 junction.

Most of the marchers were people whose land, rivers and livelihoods had been sacrificed to development projects. They included farmers, fishing communities affected by the Pak Mun dam, indigenous and ethnic communities, and urban poor facing eviction. They say dams, mines and other projects were imposed without asking people, damaging the environment and raising the country's debt.

The protesters say police kicked and pushed people and tried to detain them by tying their hands with plastic cable ties. Several people suffered minor injuries. Police kept the flyover closed until members of the human rights commission stepped in and began to arrange talks.

The network has said it will file a case against the police. The protesters spent the night camped on two lanes of Ratchadaphisek Road. In their statement they demanded accountability from the World Bank and the IMF, compensation for affected communities and an end to the intimidation of activists.

The Pak Mun dam came up again and again in this march. Built on the Mun river in north-east Thailand, this dam has for decades been a symbol of resistance by villages that depend on fish, and this protest shows that the question is still not settled.
nazar: Big financial institutions talk about development in shining halls, while the villages that pay its price are stopped outside on the road. This scene is not Thailand's alone; it is familiar from the Narmada to the Mekong.
No development can last without listening to the people affected by projects that took away their rivers and land.
sawal: Where is the chair for the uprooted at the development meeting?
ref: Pak Mun dam
A dam built on Thailand's Mun river in the 1990s, which reduced fish and deeply hurt the livelihoods of nearby fishing villages.
IMF
The International Monetary Fund, which gives loans and economic advice to countries. Its conditions are often questioned in poor countries.

h: Arundhati Roy: AI is a crime against humanity
dek: In this Democracy Now! conversation, Arundhati Roy draws on her new essay 'Apocalypse Now and Then' to explain how artificial intelligence is swallowing language, land, water and trust.
body: This is the second part of Arundhati Roy's long conversation with Democracy Now! In the first part she spoke about the culling of voter rolls in India and the young people's 'cockroach' movement. In this part Amy Goodman and Nermeen Shaikh talk to her about her essay 'Apocalypse Now and Then', published in Equator magazine. That same week Roy also spoke at the 'People's AI Summit' in New York.

Roy says the idea for the essay came when AI companies were on one hand talking about a small but real risk of humanity ending, and on the other selling that same risk to investors as a feature of their product. The more dangerous the product, the more valuable. In her view this is like a joke about buying and selling the apocalypse.

Her deepest worry is about language and literature. Publishers now look for machine writing in manuscripts, some prizes have already gone to machine-written work, and writers' books have been used without permission to train large language models. Mentioning an offer of about two thousand dollars per book in the settlement of a class action lawsuit, she calls this the privatisation of the shared history of human creativity.

Roy asks what mental confusion a society will be trapped in when there is no trust left that a word or a video truly comes from that person. And what will a new generation lose if it never struggles, never fails, never makes unfinished art?

She links AI to her old work on dams, mining and the corporate capture of resources. In her view AI companies need land, money, data, power and water, and by tying themselves to national security they want to become so big that they will not be allowed to fall. She sees a bubble in this, whose bursting will be felt far and wide.

She gives Indian examples herself. In Visakhapatnam data centres are getting approval without regard for groundwater, and local people are protesting. In remote places like Ladakh such centres could become a threat to glaciers. And Indian workers are recording their own movements so that robots can learn from them, robots that will tomorrow take their place.

In the end Roy says it is not too late to resist. People should spread information, say no to such projects and speak out loudly. Reading the end of her essay, she calls the rise of AI a crime against humanity and goes beyond the demand for regulation to take a much harder stand against the companies.
nazar: The AI debate often shrinks to office jobs and the convenience of chatbots. Roy takes it to where all this runs from: water, land, power and cheap labour, the same resources over which villages and the poor are already fighting.
It is not necessary to agree with everything she says, but the question of Visakhapatnam's groundwater and of workers training robots should not be missing from India's policy debate.
sawal: Whose glass will the data centre's water come from?
ref: Large language model
A computer system that learns from the text of billions of words and writes human-like language. Books and articles are used on a large scale in training it.
Data centre
Buildings with thousands of servers, which need huge amounts of power and water to run and keep cool.

h: Forgiveness begins where the law gives up
dek: Drawing on Jacques Derrida, Gargi Mishra asks whether only the unforgivable can be forgiven, and whether any state can forgive on behalf of the dead.
body: In this essay published in Sammukh, Gargi Mishra does not see forgiveness as an easy gift. For her it is a dark river in which a person drowns his broken shadows. Her first point is that forgiveness is often less about acquitting the wrongdoer and more about release from the burden the wounded person keeps carrying.

Then she turns to the French philosopher Jacques Derrida, who gave us deconstruction and in later years turned towards ethics and politics. The writer says that for Derrida true forgiveness is unconditional: it asks for no apology, no remorse, no promise to reform. Forgiveness resting on conditions becomes a bargain. That is why Derrida claims that only what is unforgivable can be forgiven.

The essay shows two ends of forgiveness. One is pure, ethical forgiveness, which is almost impossible in daily life; the other is practical, political forgiveness, which works within power, reconciliation and institutions. The two are different but bound together: if the ideal of the first does not survive, the second is left as mere strategy.

The most interesting part is about forgiveness by the state. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Rwanda's gacaca courts, post-war Germany apologising to Jewish communities and paying compensation, Canada's and Australia's apologies to indigenous peoples. The writer says Derrida is suspicious of all of these, because they come with conditions of confession, time limits and ritual, and the question remains of who will forgive on behalf of the dead. Many survivors refused to forgive, which shows that forgiveness cannot be imposed.
In the end she says forgiveness is neither forgetting nor consent. It is building a new relationship with memory: letting the wound stay visible, but not becoming its prisoner.
nazar: In India forgiveness often becomes a tool of politics: regret before elections, a reconciliation committee after riots, and then everything as before. This essay reminds us that the right to forgive belongs only to those who suffered injustice, not to any government or party.
In our view the most important lesson is that forgiveness cannot take the place of justice. First let the truth be recorded, and then, if someone wishes, let them forgive.
sawal: Who will forgive on behalf of those who are dead?
ref: Jacques Derrida
French philosopher (1930-2004) who gave us deconstruction, which questions fixed meanings and either-or thinking.
Truth and Reconciliation Commission
A commission set up in South Africa after apartheid ended, where a path to amnesty was kept open for those who confessed to their crimes.

h: Whoever holds the key owns the journey
dek: In Kailash Wankhede's story 'Chaabi' (The Key), a Tempo Traveller driver steers through a traffic jam, love and a caste debate breaking out in the back seats.
body: Sammukh has reprinted Kailash Wankhede's story 'Chaabi' (The Key), which first appeared in Hans in 2019. The story unfolds in a hired Tempo Traveller. The driver, Sandesh, is stuck in a jam in the rainy season, and four families sit in the vehicle who need to get there fast.

Sandesh is a restless, quick-witted young man deep in love. In the jam he gets down and phones Mukta, and soon Mukta arrives with tea in a thermos. Horns blare behind, the passengers grumble, but these few minutes are his own. From here the story begins to show the gap between those who buy time with money and those who survive by selling their time.

In the vehicle is a rich passenger in sunglasses, who flares up again and again at the delay and brushes off everything the driver says. Among the passengers a discussion starts about a doctor's suicide, which one woman links to caste discrimination, and the talk turns into a heated argument about reservation. Sandesh cuts in to say that merit is not something neutral, it is shaped by privilege, and yardsticks like height or caste are arbitrary.

After a stop at a dhaba (roadside eatery) it comes out that Sandesh was once sent back from army recruitment, where other candidates beat him up. On a winding ghat road he drives fast for a while, as if he has something to prove about death and fate, then slows down. The passenger in sunglasses decides the driver is dangerous. The story ends on the idea that the journey is in the control of the one who holds the key.

Born in Indore, Wankhede is in the Indian Administrative Service. His story collections 'Satyapan' (Verification) and 'Sulgan' (Smouldering) and novel 'Ujla Andhera' (Bright Darkness) are published by Rajkamal, and he has received the Hans Katha Samman.
nazar: On our roads, the person to whom the most lives are entrusted is the one whose opinion is heard the least. This story gives voice to the driver who quietly listens to the argument in the back and knows by which ladder those lecturing on merit climbed up. To every debate on reservation this story adds an important question: who keeps an account of the life of the man holding the steering wheel?
sawal: How easy does the merit debate seem from the back seat?
ref: Hans
A Hindi fiction magazine started by Premchand, revived from 1986 by Rajendra Yadav, which became a major platform for Dalit and women's writing.
Tempo Traveller
A small bus with twelve to fifteen seats, hired with a driver for family trips.

h: A bakery in Fort, an old magician and Kawabata's sadness
dek: Gagan Gill's memoir-essay begins with an unusual encounter in an old Mumbai bakery and moves on to life, death and the stories of Yasunari Kawabata.
body: In 'Walwala-e-Hayat' (The Thrill of Life), published in Samalochan, Gagan Gill writes that the fragrance of life comes uninvited and lingers for a long time. A damp breeze from a Mumbai lane takes her back to a morning years ago, when she was walking around the city with the writer Jaishankar, Amrit Gangar and Prakash Mudaliar.

The real story is about Yazdani Bakery in Fort, which the writer says started in 1953 and is famous for brun maska (crusty bread with butter). On the wall are old black-and-white family photos, and one handsome man appears in every picture. The writer takes a photo of the whole board. Just then a call comes from the counter: an elderly owner, who has trouble speaking, angrily asks her to delete the pictures. She deletes them in front of him.

Then she recognises that he is the same man who looks young on the wall. As soon as she says so, the old man's anger melts. He comes and sits close, spins a brun on the wooden table to make it sing near his ear, and then plays it like a mouth organ. The writer says that years later she learned from the internet that the old man she met in March 2014, Zend Merwan Zend, died in January 2021.

From here the essay turns to life and death: the young want to die, the old want to live, and neither is in our hands. Then the writer turns to the Japanese Nobel laureate Yasunari Kawabata, who took his own life in 1972. Through two of his stories, 'House of the Sleeping Beauties' and 'Yumiura', she shows how Kawabata shaped his loneliness and depression into fiction.
The essay's tone is sad, not bitter. In the end the writer says most people get used to living half a life, and still this world must have been made with great tenderness.
nazar: Our cities are made of small shops on whose walls a family's whole lifetime hangs. Gagan Gill's essay shows that photographing a stranger's wall is also an intrusion into his memory, and asking permission is not mere courtesy. In a time when old bakeries and cafes are closing, this piece reminds us that a city's real heritage is the people who kept them running.
sawal: Do you ask before photographing a stranger's wall?
ref: Yazdani Bakery
An old bakery in Mumbai's Fort area, known for brun maska and fresh pav (bread rolls).
Yasunari Kawabata
Japanese writer (1899-1972), the first Japanese to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1968, and author of 'Snow Country'.

h: Five hundred letters that were meant to be burned
dek: Hindwi's Bela has published Khalil Gibran's letters to Mary Haskell, which show how much a woman's support lay behind 'The Prophet'.
body: In the Bela section of Hindwi, under its 'Letters' series, the letters Khalil Gibran wrote to Mary Haskell have appeared in Hindi. With them comes a long introduction that tells the story of this relationship. The translator's name is not given on the page.

According to the introduction, when the two met, Gibran was a struggling 21-year-old painter and Mary was ten years older, the headmistress of a well-known girls' school in Boston. Gibran proposed marriage and Mary said no. Still she stayed with him for years: she sent him to Paris to study, taught him English, helped him with money and sat with him working on manuscripts, including 'The Prophet'.

The two mostly lived in different cities and talked through letters. When they were together, Mary recorded everything Gibran said in her diary. About 500 letters and 47 diaries went unseen by anyone for years. After Gibran's death, Barbara Young, who wrote his biography, found a box of twenty-five years of letters while sorting his papers, even though she had worked at Gibran's place for several years and knew nothing of this relationship.

Gibran wanted the letters burned. Mary first agreed, then changed her mind and took them to her home in Savannah, Georgia, where she spent her last years. Later Virginia Hilu put them together in a book called 'Beloved Prophet'.

The letters from 1908 to 1918 open up an artist's inner world. From Paris he writes of wrestling with colours and complains about the masters who want exact copying more than feeling. From New York he writes about his studio, 'Broken Wings' written in Arabic and his need for solitude, and refuses to go travelling to Cuba or Bermuda at Mary's expense.
nazar: The biographies of great writers often leave out the women who taught them, shaped them and made them fit to be published. Mary Haskell's story is just that: twenty-five years together, yet almost missing from friends' accounts and biographies. It is good that these letters have come into Hindi; if only the translator's name had been printed too, justice would be complete.
sawal: Where is Mary Haskell in the pages of 'The Prophet'?
ref: The Prophet
Gibran's English book of 1923, in which a prophet speaks in short prose poems on love, work and death.
Bela
The prose section of the Hindwi website, where columns, memoirs, letters and comments are published daily.

h: The clouds hid the moon, and Indra became a corporate boss
dek: In Hindwi's satire column 'Reel Rasacharya', Rachit sets out from a cloudy Karva Chauth night and arrives at Indra, the Eid moon and Plato.
body: Rachit's column 'Reel Rasacharya' (the reel connoisseur) on Hindwi's Bela pokes fun at society through social media reels. This time the subject is Karva Chauth (the fast wives keep for their husbands, broken on sighting the moon). The writer says the week before the festival went in watching viral videos from past years: in one, a husband in a thirty-second reel looks as helpless as women were shown for years; in another, a wife stands on one leg to show her husband's 'stability', in which the writer sees a lost talent for gymnastics.

This time the weather was the strangest. Unseasonal clouds covered the moon, those fasting had to look up moonrise time on Google and make do with the 'moon' of their own home. From here the column steps into the Puranas. Indra appears as an insecure, irritable corporate boss who cannot bear anyone's devotion. In the Gokul story the clouds had to work seven days of overtime, and the writer wonders whether the wives of those clouds were left waiting with their karva (the clay pot of the fast).

Then the moon connects to Eid. The writer reminds us that in Pakistan the moon committee did not see the moon and Eid was fixed for the next day, but in Peshawar a poet saw the moon, which became a joke in the media. On this pretext he pokes fun at Plato's view that poets have no place in the ideal state: poets call the beloved the moon and want the whole world to celebrate when she appears.

In the end the moon itself looks like an underappreciated employee, who has sat at the same desk for years working without complaint. The writer says that in north India it is remembered on just two days, Eid and Karva Chauth. On other days it is watched by lovers sitting on rooftops, or by fans of the Raj Kapoor and Nargis song in 'Awara'.
nazar: Karva Chauth has moved out of the courtyard and become a festival of reels and advertisements. Rachit's satire laughs at this change, but also shows that Eid and Karva Chauth are tied to the wait for the same moon. In a time when there is a race to divide festivals, reminding us that the moon in the sky belongs to everyone is no small thing.
sawal: If clouds cover the moon, on whose word should the fast be broken?
ref: The Govardhan story
According to legend, Krishna held up Mount Govardhan for seven days to save Gokul from the downpour sent by Indra.
Moon committee
Pakistan's official Ruet-e-Hilal Committee, which announces the sighting of the moon for Ramzan and Eid and is often in controversy.

h: A mother in the exam hall the day after giving birth
dek: In Indira Dangi's story 'Bhagya Vidhata' (Maker of Destiny), a new daughter-in-law holds on to her resolve to finish her BEd amid the cruelties of her in-laws' home.
body: Indira Dangi's story 'Bhagya Vidhata', published on Shabdankan, begins in the flat of a joint family, where the new daughter-in-law Deepti has arrived with her dowry trunk. Her sisters-in-law Chanchal and Kanchan grab the good things at once, and her mother-in-law Veni asks for her rings on the pretext of showing them to guests and returns one short. Deepti stays silent, because pointing a finger at her mother-in-law would make her an outsider forever.

Things were no different at her parents' home. Her mother always put her brothers Manu and Pradeep first and refused to pay Deepti's BEd fees. Only her father quietly stood by her. She took admission anyway and carried housework, college and preparation for the teacher eligibility test, all three at once.

At her in-laws' she toils like a servant. When she studies in the drawing room at night, her mother-in-law orders sweet puris made at midnight. So she starts studying in the bathroom and writes notes on her palm and wrist. When she becomes pregnant, the family pressures her to have a sex test. Deepti flatly refuses and, remembering the discrimination of her own childhood, decides that if she has a daughter she will give her a better life.

The turn comes just before her final BEd exam. Labour pains begin, a daughter is born in a government hospital and the in-laws go back home. Weak as she is, Deepti begs a nurse to get her to the exam centre thirty-five kilometres away. The doctor first refuses, then after about two hours a vehicle is arranged and a sanitation worker goes along with mother and baby. She arrives fifteen minutes late, the examiners let her sit, and she keeps writing her answers while feeding the baby now and then.

The story does not give the result; it leaves open the question of whether Deepti will be able to write her own destiny. Indira Dangi, principal of a government college in Madhya Pradesh, has stories taught in the syllabus of several universities.
nazar: If Deepti's story seems made up, look at the newspapers: every year somewhere a woman is seen taking an exam a few hours after giving birth, and the news is about her courage, not about the home that pushed her to this state. Families that treat education as a favour and the mindset that frowns on a daughter are both still alive.
In our view the story's most important character is the sanitation worker who goes along. Women's battles are often made easier by just such nameless women.
sawal: Notes written on a palm bear witness to what kind of home?
ref: BEd
Bachelor of Education, the two-year professional course needed to become a school teacher.
Teacher eligibility test
TET, the exam one must pass to get a teacher's job in government schools.
